title: A disabled theatre troupe makes the able-bodied the discriminated minority — and it isn't asking for your sympathy
dek: Yaoyao flips the whole social order: after a nuclear war most people are augmented, and the few unmodified able-bodied are the ones born in sin, the ones who have to fight for their rights. This isn't a lament — it's a power fantasy written for disabled people.
why: Mostly oral testimony, with no data or research framework; its value is in specific scenes and in how one play grew. Anyone looking for methodology or industry judgment can skip it.
who: People in nonprofits, theatre and community workshops; content people who want to understand why inclusion can't rest on goodwill alone; practitioners and volunteers working on disability issues.
skip: The rehearsal clip at the start and the submission pitch at the end can be skipped.

points.h: Disabled women being unable to leave the house is the norm
points.body: Yaoyao's earliest work was the documentary Han Ya (寒鸦), about three disabled women's struggles with family education and employment. One of them, a woman in her thirties, had not left her home in 36 years; when her parents took her out to visit relatives at holidays, it felt to her ‘like walking a little dog or cat’. Later she got the first computer of her life, went online, and found a job as a telephone operator — no degree required, only a sweet voice. Once she had the job she bought herself a wheelchair and rolled out of the house. Another woman, a visually impaired mother, was allowed to breastfeed her newborn for only five minutes before her mother-in-law took the baby away, on the grounds that ‘you can't see, you can't raise a child’; for years afterward she fought her husband's family for custody. These accounts made Yaoyao realise that being unable to leave the house was not an isolated case.

points.h: Disabled people's friends are all disabled people
points.body: A former colleague of Yaoyao's uses a wheelchair. When she moved house she could only ask friends who also use wheelchairs, loading the chairs front and back and hauling everything load by load. Yaoyao instinctively asked why she didn't call able-bodied friends who can walk upright to help — it would be done in half a day. The colleague paused, then said, I don't know any able-bodied people. She did not have a single able-bodied friend; even her friends all used wheelchairs. Yaoyao says she didn't know how to continue the conversation, and realised only one thing: if disabled and able-bodied people never even get the chance to meet, ‘you have no chance at inclusion at all’. That was the direct starting point for her later search for a drama teacher and for making integrated theatre.

points.h: Writing the able-bodied as the discriminated ones born in sin
points.body: The troupe Leyi's first play, Reverse Future (逆转未来), does a straight identity reversal: a nuclear war turns most people disabled, and they become new humans through technological modification — electronic eyes, cochlear implants and the like. The remaining able-bodied minority, because of ‘the crime of starting the nuclear war’, become the ones born in sin, marginalised by society. Yaoyao's logic: since she herself is a person with situs inversus, she might as well flip the whole society too, turning the rights disabled people now have to fight for into rights the able-bodied have to fight for. She calls it writing a power fantasy for disabled people. The plot's core: an original-sin father, to spare his son the suffering of an able-bodied body, gets drunk, picks up a chainsaw and tries to cut off his son's legs, but ends up in a pool of blood himself; the son is charged with patricide, and the courtroom scenes open up the debate about original-sin people and augmented people.

points.h: How the unseen and the unheard partner up
points.body: Visually impaired actor Wang Xiaomin was pulled in by deaf actor Li Ning during an audition to be his partner. His first reaction was blank: you can't hear, I can't see, how do we act. Li Ning's solution was to put his hand on the back of Wang's hand and trace, tapping once when it was Wang's line. Director Ma Yan says this form already exists abroad, with blind and deaf performers on the same stage: the deaf person's hand rests on the visually impaired person's hand, and the visually impaired person can feel the movements. Wang Xiaomin says deaf people had been around him since childhood, but back then he saw them as two kinds of people born with communication barriers, ‘absolutely impossible to communicate’, a barrier that was almost insurmountable — after this collaboration he and Li Ning became very good friends. The troupe also had to solve sign language interpretation, real-time captioning on a big screen, and assigning a volunteer to each visually impaired actor for audio description.

points.h: Visually impaired actors cheat on stage with earphones
points.body: Only later in rehearsals did the director discover that the visually impaired actors were in fact ‘cheating’: they wore earphones, listened to their lines at several times normal speed, and delivered them live on stage without a hitch. The director had no way to assess this and could only wonder how the visually impaired actors got their lines down so fast. Conversely, the director doesn't know sign language and could only watch everyone signing while laughing along, when in fact the actors might be complaining about him in sign. Once they got familiar, everyone knew each other's little tricks.

points.h: She received the best production award from the ICU
points.body: In 2024 Reverse Future was selected for the Nanjing New Theatre Festival initiated by Stan Lai. That year Yaoyao had heart problems and was admitted to the ICU; the troupe nearly fell apart, and a friend stepped in to gather everyone for rehearsals and take them to Nanjing. At the closing buffet, while the other groups' tables sat empty and their members dressed up waiting for the awards, only their table kept going back for more food, thinking ‘how could it possibly be us’. In the end they won Best Production, the festival's highest award, and jury chairman Stan Lai stood and led the applause. The news reached the ICU at the same moment as the award, and Yaoyao lay in her hospital bed in tears. That October the play was invited to the Wuzhen Theatre Festival as the first integrated disability production, the only piece in the ‘Nothing Is Impossible’ section.

points.h: After writing this play, she changed her answer on being born
points.body: The second play, I Choose to Be Born (我选择出生), is set in a world where every country legislates that when a fetus reaches eight months, parents must use brainwaves to inform it of its health and family circumstances, and the fetus decides whether to be born. Among five families: deaf parents who must honestly tell their child you'll be deaf too; a husband who deceives his wife into having a child; a family that favours boys over girls; and a final story adapted from Yaoyao's own experience. The troupe's actors couldn't get through the script, because their life experiences were eerily similar — only the conditions differed. Asked whether they would still choose to be born if they had it to do over, most of the troupe still said yes, because they still love this world; Yaoyao changed her answer: she used to say she would choose to be born, but now she might choose not to be, because disabled people are forced to be born into this society, with no choice at all.

points.h: Cai Cong and she give opposite answers to the same question
points.body: The episode sets the deaf couple in I Choose to Be Born against the real Cai Cong (蔡聪): Cai Cong and his wife are both visually impaired, and when his wife was pregnant many people urged them to get tests to see whether the child would inherit the visual impairment, but Cai Cong did not want to presume that such a life was not worth starting merely because the child might also be visually impaired; they believe they can give a child a loving family. The deaf couple in the play decide to let the child be born. Yaoyao and Cai Cong give very different answers, and the argument over this choice persists. The question the episode poses: when a family makes a choice, how much choice do they actually have.

This play makes you think. The sincerity of the performance covers the flaws in technique. What is most striking is the troupe's refusal to be pitied.
